GUARDIAN is progressing with both of its validation partners: MONSSON in the energy sector and Hyperfy (GOC) in physical security. Both strands apply the same idea: smaller models, including small language models (SLMs), running on modest, CPU-first infrastructure close to the data, with a human operator making every decision. GUARDIAN started on 1 July 2026, and its six-month implementation runs to 31 December 2026. documents.t: With MONSSON, GUARDIAN is working on SLM-based second-opinion agents for energy-sector operations centers, in renewable-storage and virtual-power-plant monitoring scenarios. Such an agent is designed to review monitoring alerts and give the operator a second opinion: what it noticed, why, and how uncertain it is. The operator decides what, if anything, to do. Each agent is a workload under the GUARDIAN benchmark, to be measured for latency, data locality and resource footprint across low-power edge, low-end VPS, local-server and central/cloud profiles. This is GUARDIAN's primary validation route. More on the energy-sector use case.

This is a demonstrator, not a deployment in a partner's live operations center. Candidate tasks include alarm clustering, false-alarm review and event summarization. More on the operations-center use case.

Generating a single image with a modern AI model takes about as much energy as fully charging your smartphone. Furthermore, if you extrapolate that out to the sheer volume of prompts, generations, and automated tasks happening globally every single second, it paints a pretty terrifying picture: we are looking at these sprawling, hyper-cooled server farms out in the desert. They're consuming the electrical equivalent of entire mid-sized nations. The wild thing is that the tech industry has essentially accepted this as a given, treating the massive carbon footprint as basically an unavoidable tax on progress. We've decided that artificial intelligence is inherently this giant, centralized, power-hungry machine—a total brute-force approach to innovation. It's like we took the mindset of the Industrial Revolution and slapped it onto data processing: you want a smarter model, just build a bigger data center, buy massive compute clusters, and pump more gigawatts of power into the cooling systems. The whole architecture is completely addicted to centralized scale. ... documents.s: Sustainable Edge AI on Local CPUs

documents.t: The project stands for Green, User-guided, Auditable Resource-aware Deployment for Industrial AI Networks, a dense acronym that serves as a perfect roadmap for what the project is trying to achieve technically. Our ELIAS-based project proposed a six-month, 10 person-month sprint to deliver a reusable toolkit and benchmark specifically designed to run operational AI on commodity edge nodes and low-end virtual private servers, or VPSs. This is an architectural rebellion: a shift away from GPUs. We are so used to the paradigm that running AI requires massive GPU clusters. The whole industry is obsessed with buying every available GPU to train and run these monolithic models, but GUARDIAN proposed something completely countercultural—CPU-first, smaller-model inference. The mechanical differences between the hardware explain why this is such a big deal. The AI industry shifted heavily to GPUs around 2012 because of their architecture. A GPU is essentially thousands of tiny, relatively weak processing cores that execute simple mathematical operations simultaneously. This massive parallelization is perfect for the heavy matrix multiplication required to train deep neural networks, but the trade-off is massive: GPUs consume a staggering amount of electricity, require intense thermal cooling, and are incredibly expensive to purchase and operate. By contrast, a CPU, or central processing unit, does not have thousands of cores; it might have 8, 16, or 32 highly complex, incredibly fast cores. If a GPU is an army of 10,000 middle schoolers doing basic arithmetic all at once, a CPU is a room full of 10 genius-level professors solving complex sequential logic puzzles one at a time, incredibly fast. CPUs are everywhere—in every standard server, every laptop, and every piece of industrial equipment. They are cheap, and their power consumption is a fraction of that of a GPU array. GUARDIAN is essentially betting that specific localized AI tasks, such as anomaly detection in an industrial setting, do not need an army of 10,000 middle schoolers in a centralized cloud. You can use the professors already sitting in the server rack next to the machinery, running a smaller, highly focused model directly on the local CPU and completely bypassing the massive energy tax of cloud computing. What made the GUARDIAN proposal so compelling to the ELIAS evaluators was its restraint: the documents are extremely careful to state explicitly that we are not making wild, unverified carbon-reduction claims. Instead of making grandiose claims, GUARDIAN focuses strictly on reporting resource-footprint proxies. In practice, we are building a methodology to measure data locality, meaning trying to mathematically prove how much energy is saved by keeping data on the local factory floor rather than transmitting gigabytes of telemetry data across the internet to a centralized server. The transmission alone costs energy. GUARDIAN also measures execution latency and serving patterns on these low-power edge nodes, building a localized evidence base against which sustainability hypotheses can be tested. The leverage is our existing technology, and our proposal made it clear that we are using the proprietary Ratio1 platform as the foundation. A bounded monitoring workload is an AI system given a very strict, highly localized task, such as watching time-series data from a specific industrial system for anomalies that indicate something is about to break or go wrong. The critical psychological barrier in high-stakes environments, such as managing a national energy grid or securing a physical facility, is fear of autonomous action. Enterprise buyers are fundamentally terrified of black-box AI. They do not want an algorithm making an unexplainable decision that automatically shuts down a power plant or locks a corporate headquarters without human intervention; they want what the documents call an advisory-only system. They want a system that raises its hand and says: "I have noticed a 14% anomalous drop in voltage on turbine number four over the last 20 minutes. Based on my local model, I am 87% confident this represents a failing capacitor. Here is the specific data stream that led me to this conclusion. You, the human operator, need to look at this." It is the fundamental difference between hiring an autonomous CEO and hiring a diligent intern. GUARDIAN is essentially selling the enterprise market the ultimate AI intern: it stays awake 24 hours a day, seven days a week, tirelessly reviewing mountains of incredibly boring time-series data. It flags anomalies and, crucially, leaves a meticulous, mathematically sound audit trail of its work right on your desk, but it never makes the final executive decision. That auditability is the entire ball game for enterprise adoption. By providing clear confidence signals, uncertainty metrics, and a transparent audit trail, GUARDIAN aims to address the trust issue, which its planned validation is designed to test. From a purely strategic go-to-market perspective, this creates an incredibly low-friction commercial route for our startup. Achieving TRL 5 validation gives GUARDIAN the exact evidence class that its broader commercial strategy, our Ratio1 RedMesh flagship product (https://redmesh.ai), is currently only touching. In that sales cycle, a corporate customer does not have to authorize a multi-million-dollar overhaul of its entire IT infrastructure, upload all its highly sensitive proprietary data to a centralized cloud controlled by a tech giant, or surrender operational control to a machine. Instead, the customer can begin with a bounded technical assessment, buy a cheap localized CPU server, install the GUARDIAN edge software or a modular piece of its framework, and run the AI intern in parallel with existing systems. It can inspect the evidence pack, review the audit trail, and slowly build organizational trust in the technology before committing to a full deployment. It is a brilliant Trojan horse strategy for getting AI into hesitant legacy industries. Our proposal outlined two specific contexts for validating this highly efficient, auditable, edge-based anomaly-detection toolkit. The primary focus is the energy sector, where GUARDIAN is partnering with MONSSON to monitor renewable-energy storage and virtual power plants. The secondary pilot is an operations-center co-piloting demonstrator focused on physical-security workflows, partnered with a company called Hyperfy or GOC. Energy grids and physical security are therefore its initial proving grounds.

This leaves a massive structural question about where all of this is heading. If this architecture works, if GUARDIAN proves that highly complex, highly accurate anomaly detection can run on cheap localized CPUs without a massive data center, it completely upends the accepted narrative of the tech industry, with profound implications for the future of operational infrastructure. The GUARDIAN proposal highlighted an intentional shift away from the centralized cloud and back to the localized edge, as a hypothesis that its planned measurements are designed to test. If this highly auditable, tiny-model approach succeeds at scale and becomes the standard for how enterprises adopt AI in daily operations, are we looking at the beginning of the end of the cloud era for specialized artificial intelligence? What happens to the balance of power in the global technology industry when every manufacturing plant, every hospital, every local server rack, and every corporate operations center can run its own completely private, highly sustainable AI—one that requires a fraction of the electricity and never has to communicate with a tech giant's centralized desert server farm? It decentralizes the entire ecosystem, strips leverage from massive cloud providers, and puts the power of machine learning directly back into the hands of local operators, with absolute privacy and a potentially lower carbon footprint, a hypothesis that GUARDIAN's planned measurements are designed to test rather than a demonstrated result. It is a phenomenal counter-narrative to everything we are told about the future of this technology. The massive hyper-cooled server farm might not be the inevitable endgame after all. The future of daily operational AI might be a quiet, highly efficient CPU sitting in the corner of your office, diligently auditing your systems, keeping your data completely private, and leaving a paper trail for you to review in the morning.

GUARDIAN — Green, User-guided, Auditable Resource-aware Deployment for Industrial AI Networks — is a six-month project run by Naeural SRL (Ratio1). It started on 1 July 2026 and runs to 31 December 2026, with financial support from the ELIAS 2nd FSTP Open Call. The project is building a reusable toolkit and benchmark for resource-aware operational AI on commodity edge nodes and low-end virtual private servers (VPS). It tests CPU-first, smaller-model inference — including small language models (SLMs) — for operational monitoring workloads: the continuous, always-on inference that watches a process or a site and flags what a human should look at. The question is practical: can a selected operational workload run usefully on modest CPU infrastructure close to the data, instead of defaulting to centralized, GPU-heavy infrastructure? GUARDIAN answers it by measurement rather than assumption. Its common benchmark protocol compares latency, data transfer and locality, and resource-footprint proxies across low-power edge, low-end VPS, local-server and central/cloud profiles. Environmental benefits are measured, not assumed: the project does not claim carbon reductions without a defensible emissions method.

GUARDIAN applies the same toolkit and benchmark in two operational contexts: Energy sector, with MONSSON — the primary validation route: SLM-based second-opinion agents for renewable-storage and virtual-power-plant monitoring. See Energy-Sector Advisory Monitoring. Physical security, with Hyperfy (GOC) — a bounded operations-center co-pilot demonstrator focused on efficient SLM deployment. See Operations-Center Co-Pilot. Both scenarios are advisory-only: operators stay in control, with no live asset control, automated enforcement, live dispatch or biometric identification.

GUARDIAN starts at technology readiness level (TRL) 4: the underlying Ratio1 components have been validated at component level, while the integrated toolkit and benchmark are still to be validated as a complete system in an industrially relevant environment. The project targets TRL 5 through validation in the MONSSON and Hyperfy scenarios. TRL 5 is a target, not a result. See Objectives for the five goals GUARDIAN is working toward, and Expected Outputs for what the project will publish.

GUARDIAN pursues five objectives over its six-month project period (July–December 2026): Build the toolkit. Build a reusable, resource-aware Ratio1 toolkit for deploying and operating selected operational AI workloads on commodity edge and low-end VPS infrastructure. Define the benchmark protocol. Specify a common, repeatable protocol that uses a scenario-workload pair as its unit of measurement and records latency, data transfer or locality, resource-footprint proxies, audit records and human-review status across execution profiles — low-power edge, low-end VPS, local server, and central/cloud. Validate in the energy sector. Validate the toolkit in a primary renewable-storage or virtual-power-plant monitoring context with MONSSON, using approved partner, derived or synthetic data. Demonstrate transfer. Show that the same toolkit and benchmark transfer to one bounded operations-center co-pilot scenario for physical-security workflows with Hyperfy (GOC). Deliver a results handover package. Package the benchmark protocol, toolkit prototype, validation reports, public summary, demo video and data specifications so the results can be reused beyond the project, including by ELIAS. Both validation scenarios are advisory-only: operators stay in control, with no live asset control, automated enforcement, live dispatch or biometric identification. See Expected Outputs for how these objectives map to concrete outputs, and the Work Plan for timing.

GUARDIAN will deliver the following outputs by the end of the project period on 31 December 2026: Benchmark protocol — the common measurement protocol for comparing resource footprint and output across execution profiles, with a data-contract template. Toolkit prototype — the resource-aware Ratio1 edge/VPS toolkit with reproducible configuration notes. Validation reports — the primary validation report for the energy sector with MONSSON and the operations-center co-pilot demonstrator report with Hyperfy (GOC). Data specifications — data contracts, dataset cards and synthetic-data generation specifications and, where partner, privacy, IP and licensing permissions allow, a small non-sensitive data package. Final report, public summary and demo video — the project's final account of its approach and findings, a plain-language summary and a short demonstration. Handover package — the combined outputs, packaged for reuse of the results beyond the project. Any published data is limited to synthetic, anonymized, aggregated or partner-approved derived examples. The only security media published are 19 cropped camera frames of alerts tagged as false alarms, released with written permission as the GUARDIAN Second Opinion Dataset 1, public subset. Raw operational data and incident records are not published. The project starts from technology readiness level (TRL) 4 and targets TRL 5 through validation in an industrially relevant environment. TRL 5 is a target, not a claim of current maturity. Outputs approved for public release will be published on the Results & Downloads page. See Deliverables for how they map to D1–D5.

ELIAS — the European Lighthouse of AI for Sustainability — is a European research project on sustainable and trustworthy AI. It is funded by the European Union's Horizon Europe research and innovation programme under grant agreement No. 101120237 and brings together research partners working on AI systems that are efficient, transparent, and aligned with European values. ELIAS runs open calls that provide financial support to third parties (FSTP) — see The 2nd Open Call & FSTP — to fund focused projects that extend ELIAS's research into new applications and contexts. GUARDIAN received financial support through the 2nd Open Call. GUARDIAN's relationship to ELIAS is one of reuse and handover of results: GUARDIAN takes ELIAS research themes on sustainable and trustworthy AI as a starting point, applies them in operational scenarios, and hands its outputs back for reuse. It is not an integration into, certification against, or deployment inside ELIAS's own systems. See the Evaluation Result page for GUARDIAN's outcome in the call. More information on ELIAS is available at elias-ai.eu.

GUARDIAN is a Naeural SRL (Ratio1) project supported through the ELIAS 2nd FSTP Open Call, in which its proposal ranked 2nd with a score of 8.86. The project started on 1 July 2026, and its six-month implementation runs to 31 December 2026. The ranking is published by ELIAS in the official ranking list of the 2nd Open Call. GUARDIAN's relationship to ELIAS is one of reuse and handover of results: GUARDIAN takes ELIAS research themes on sustainable and trustworthy AI as a starting point, applies them in operational scenarios, and hands its outputs back for reuse. It is not an integration into, certification against, or deployment inside ELIAS's own systems. See What is ELIAS? for more on ELIAS.

ELIAS's open calls provide financial support to third parties (FSTP) — a mechanism used by Horizon Europe projects to fund external organizations through a competitive, evaluated application process, extending the funding project's research reach without requiring every participant to be a named consortium partner. The 2nd Open Call invited proposals for focused projects that build on and extend ELIAS's research on sustainable and trustworthy AI. Proposals were evaluated and ranked by ELIAS against the call's published criteria. GUARDIAN received financial support through this call. The project started on 1 July 2026, and its six-month implementation runs to 31 December 2026. See Evaluation Result for GUARDIAN's outcome in the call.

GUARDIAN's toolkit is being built on Ratio1, a decentralized edge AI platform. Ratio1 edge nodes are designed to run containerized AI workloads close to where data is produced, rather than shipping data to a central data center for every inference. Many Ratio1 components are published on GitHub; licence and release terms vary by repository. Public sources for the platform: Website: ratio1.ai Source code: github.com/ratio1 GUARDIAN uses the Ratio1 platform as the execution layer for its toolkit; see Toolkit & Benchmark for how GUARDIAN's own components fit on top of it.

The toolkit and benchmark are organized around scenario-workload pairs: a monitoring scenario (what is being watched, and what a human operator needs to know) paired with a concrete inference workload (the model and task that produces that information). Scenarios are operationally motivated; their inputs are approved partner data, derived data or synthetic data. GUARDIAN's workloads are designed around smaller models running CPU-first, including small language models (SLMs) — for example, second-opinion agents in the energy-sector validation and an operations-center co-pilot in the physical-security demonstrator. See the use cases for both scenarios.

Each scenario-workload pair is to be measured across multiple execution profiles, so the same workload's resource/quality trade-off is comparable across hardware tiers: Low-power edge Low-end virtual private server (VPS) Local server Central/cloud

The benchmark protocol is designed to record, per execution profile, latency, data transfer or locality, and resource-footprint proxies — such as model size, inference time, CPU and memory use, or an available energy proxy — alongside the workload's output. These proxies are reported as measured; they are not converted into carbon-reduction claims without a defensible emissions method.

Each benchmark run is designed to log audit fields alongside its output, including the reported confidence or uncertainty signal, an explanation field and human-review status, so that a reviewer can see what the model reported, how uncertain it said it was, and whether a human has reviewed the result.

A monitoring workload runs on a Ratio1 edge node; the node's output is captured by benchmark logging (resource footprint and audit fields); logged runs accumulate into an audit trail that supports later review.

Validation partner: MONSSON · Status: in progress · Report: D3, planned for November 2026 This is GUARDIAN's primary validation route. It applies the GUARDIAN toolkit and benchmark to advisory monitoring in the renewable-storage and virtual-power-plant (VPP) space: watching operational data from storage and generation assets and surfacing what a human operator should look at.

With MONSSON, GUARDIAN is working on SLM-based second-opinion agents for energy-sector operations centers. A second-opinion agent uses a small language model (SLM) running on modest, CPU-first infrastructure. It is designed to review monitoring alerts — for example from anomaly detection or forecast-error monitoring — and to give the operator an explanation and an uncertainty signal alongside its view. The operator decides what, if anything, to do.

The validation is planned to cover at least two renewable-storage or VPP scenario-workload pairs, using approved partner, derived or synthetic data. For each, the benchmark protocol is designed to record latency, data locality, resource-footprint proxies, uncertainty and audit indicators, together with the advisory-use boundaries and limitations observed.

This use case is advisory-only. It does not control live energy assets, does not take automated enforcement actions, and does not perform biometric identification of any kind. Its output is information for a human operator to review and act on, not an autonomous control signal. Raw operational data is not published. Measured results for this use case will be published on Results & Downloads once approved for release.

Validation partner: Hyperfy (GOC) · Status: in progress · Report: D4, planned for November 2026 This use case is designed to demonstrate transfer of the GUARDIAN toolkit and benchmark to a structurally different context: an operations-center co-pilot that surfaces relevant information from operational feeds to a human operator in a physical-security setting. It is one bounded demonstrator, built on the same toolkit and benchmark as the energy-sector validation.

With Hyperfy (GOC), GUARDIAN is working on efficient deployment of small language models (SLMs): running small models on CPU-first edge and VPS infrastructure, to be demonstrated in one bounded co-pilot scenario for a physical-security operations center; the benchmark is designed to measure the resources this takes. This is a demonstrator, not a deployment in a partner's live operations center. Candidate tasks include alarm clustering, false-alarm review, event summarization, incident-note drafting and response-queue explanation.

The demonstrator uses metadata, derived events, anonymized examples or synthetic scenarios. Raw security media is used only with written approval. One set of examples from this pilot is public: 19 camera frames of alerts that were tagged as false alarms, cropped to remove the text strips and published with written permission under the CC BY-NC 4.0 licence as the GUARDIAN Second Opinion Dataset 1, public subset. The 19 frames were selected to show no person and no readable number plate, name or logo. No other security media, dispatch logs or incident records are published.

This use case is advisory-only. It does not perform biometric identification of any kind, does not take automated enforcement actions, does not dispatch interventions, and does not control live assets. Its output is information for a human operator to review and act on, not an autonomous control signal. Measured results for this use case will be published on Results & Downloads once approved for release.
